justice: Most of the corridor width is allocated to a single vehicular carriageway, while no dedicated sidewalk is visibly provided on either side.
Raised curbs edge both sides of the road, but there are no visible curb ramps, tactile paving, or marked crossing points to support broad user access.
The long walled edge on the right and enclosed compound edge on the left suggest limited public frontage and few shared amenities for different road users.
The street appears usable mainly for motorists because the centerline organizes vehicle movement, while equivalent pedestrian and cycling facilities are absent.
safety: The roadway is narrow and appears low-speed, which can help reduce severe vehicle conflicts.
A clear yellow centerline provides basic directional order for drivers on this straight segment.
There is no visible separated sidewalk or protected cycling lane, creating potential conflict if pedestrians or cyclists use the carriageway.
Long blank walls and very limited active frontage reduce natural surveillance, which can weaken perceived personal security.
livability: The corridor appears quiet and green at the edges, but it lacks visible shops, seating, or community-facing uses that support everyday street life.
The tall blank wall on the right creates an inactive edge that contributes little to social interaction or neighborhood vitality.
No pedestrians, cyclists, transit stops, or public gathering features are visible, suggesting limited support for daily social use.
Landscaping is present along both sides, but the street functions more like a service or access road than a lively public place.
sustainability: Rows of trees and planted shrubs on both sides add greenery and provide some ecological value.
The absence of visible bike lanes, transit facilities, or multimodal infrastructure limits support for low-carbon travel choices.
Continuous planted strips along the curbs may offer some stormwater absorption compared with a fully paved edge.
The street surface is dominated by asphalt roadway space, which still reflects an auto-oriented design pattern.
aesthetics: The continuous stone wall on the right gives the street a strong and coherent visual identity.
Tree lines and low shrubs soften the corridor and improve the visual quality of an otherwise hard-edged space.
The pavement appears clean and well maintained, with fresh lane markings and little visible clutter.
However, the long blank wall also creates monotony and reduces visual richness at eye level.
comfort: Street trees and shrubs provide some greenery and limited shade, improving thermal comfort compared with a fully exposed road.
The road surface looks smooth and even, which supports comfortable travel for drivers and cyclists.
There are no visible benches, shelters, or dedicated pedestrian resting areas, reducing comfort for non-motorized users.
The enclosed walls and empty character may create some psychological discomfort due to isolation despite the low apparent traffic volume.
walkability: No continuous sidewalk is visible, so pedestrians would likely need to walk close to or within the vehicular carriageway.
Raised curbs separate planting from the road, but they do not create a clearly usable walking path.
There are no visible crosswalks, curb ramps, or pedestrian signs to support connected walking routes.
The greenery improves the walking atmosphere somewhat, but the inactive walls and lack of destinations weaken pedestrian appeal.
bikeability: The corridor is relatively calm and straight, which may make casual cycling possible under light traffic conditions.
There is no dedicated or protected bike lane, so cyclists would have to share the narrow roadway with motor vehicles.
No bicycle markings, bike parking, or cycling wayfinding are visible.
Raised curbs and planted edges leave little recovery space if cyclists need to avoid passing vehicles.
